o1.said: Polymorphism: one call, many types. And two rules for using it well.

a1.said: In three p p, a box, a lamp and a whole group of parts all enter the scene through the same function.

a2.said: It takes a pointer to an Object3D, the base class.

a3.said: A mesh is an Object3D. So is a light, and so is a group. That is inheritance.

v1.said: Now a loop asks every child the same question: what type are you? The loop only knows the base class.

v2.said: But type is a virtual function, and each class overrides it.

v3.said: So the object's own type decides which one runs, while the program is running.

v4.said: That is polymorphism. Code written for the base class works with every class derived from it, even one that is written later.

l1.said: But inheriting is also a promise. Wherever code expects the base class, your class must work, without surprises.

l2.said: Here is the classic trap. This function sets a rectangle's width, then its height.

l3.said: It trusts that one does not change the other.

l4.said: In maths, a square is a rectangle. So let Square inherit, and keep its own rule: the sides stay equal.

l5.said: Now hand the function a square. It compiles.

l6.said: But setting the height also changed the width, and the caller gets the wrong shape.

l7.said: The compiler checks that the functions exist. It cannot check the promise.

l8.said: This is the Liskov substitution principle: a derived object must be able to stand in for its base.

l9.said: A derived class keeps the promise when it accepts what the base accepts, does what the base's function is meant to do, and keeps what the base guarantees.

l10.said: The fix is not a smarter square. Square and Rectangle are siblings: both are shapes, and neither stands in for the other.

c1.said: So ask before you inherit: can my class honestly stand in for the base, everywhere?

c2.said: If not, or if you only want to use what another class can do, hold it as a member instead.

c3.said: A thermostat uses a temperature sensor. It is not one. Inherit, and the sensor's functions become the thermostat's too. As a member, the sensor stays private.

c4.said: That is composition: has a, not is a. three p p does it too. A mesh is an Object3D, but it has a geometry, and it has a material.

c5.said: So any shape goes with any material, and you can swap either one while the program runs.

c6.said: With inheritance, every combination would need a class of its own.

k1.said: Polymorphism gives one call many types. Inherit when your class can stand in for its base. When you only want to reuse, compose.
